input.question: Who is Elisiv of Kyiv's spouse?

documents.text: In the midst of the 11th century, when the Viking Age was slowly giving way to the dawn of a new era, two powerful figures emerged in the realms of Norway and Kyiv. Elisiv, a princess of Kyiv, and Harald III, the King of Norway, would soon find their lives intertwined in a union that would shape the course of history. Elisiv, born into the royal family of Kyiv, was no stranger to the intricacies of politics and diplomacy. Her father, Yaroslav the Wise, had forged alliances with the great powers of Europe, and Elisiv had grown up surrounded by the trappings of power and the whispers of statecraft. As she matured, her beauty and intelligence caught the attention of suitors from across the continent. Meanwhile, in Norway, Harald III, also known as Harald Hardrada, had risen to power through a series of military campaigns and strategic alliances. His reputation as a fierce warrior and cunning leader had earned him the respect and fear of his contemporaries. As he consolidated his power, Harald set his sights on securing a marriage that would cement his position and expand his influence. It was against this backdrop that the paths of Elisiv and Harald converged. The exact circumstances of their meeting are lost to the annals of time, but historians agree that the two were married in the early 1040s. The union was a calculated move, designed to strengthen the bonds between Norway and Kyiv, and to secure a powerful ally in the region. One of the earliest recorded references to Elisiv's marriage to Harald can be found in the Icelandic Sagas, medieval texts that chronicle the history of the Viking Age. The Saga of Harald Hardrada, written in the 13th century, explicitly states that Harald married Elisiv, the daughter of Yaroslav of Kyiv. This account is corroborated by the Russian Primary Chronicle, a contemporaneous source that confirms Elisiv's parentage and her marriage to the Norwegian king. Further evidence of the marriage can be gleaned from the archaeological record. Excavations at the Viking Age settlement of Kaupang, in southern Norway, have uncovered artifacts that suggest a strong cultural exchange between Norway and Kyiv during the 11th century. The presence of Eastern European ceramics and jewelry, alongside Norse artifacts, points to a period of intense cultural and economic exchange, which would have been facilitated by the marriage of Elisiv and Harald.
